The HDPA issued an opinion requested by the Supreme Council For Civil Personnel Selection (ASEP) on the basis of Article 36 GDPR regarding the online publication of tables with the ranking and the appointment of candidates for civil service positions.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued a non-binding opinion under Article 58(3) GDPR regarding the lawfulness of processing of a photograph. The IP clarified that a photograph can be considered personal data, especially when a photo depicts an individual clearly and unambiguously allowing for their identification. Such processing must be based on a consent under Article 6(1)(a) GDPR collected in advance of such processing.

The President of the Personal Data Protection Office in Poland (PUODO) decided to discontinue proceedings concerning the processing of data in connection with the requirement for Polish judges and prosecutors to submit declarations about their membership in associations. The PUODO clarified that the obligation to submit the above mentioned statements clearly results from the provisions of the national law and thus falls under one of the legal grounds in Article 6(1)(c) GDPR. The President of the Personal Data Protection Office (UODO) stated that he cannot make a decision regarding the constitutionality of such an obligation providing that this is a competence of the Constitutional Tribunal. The Ombudsman has the right to submit motions on the compliance of acts with the Polish Constitution to the Constitutional Tribunal.
The AEPD fined a controller for not providing its users with complete information regarding the use of cookies.

A requester asked the ICO under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 for information on pay progression reviews and three versions of a data analysis report for the Pay Consistency Panel. The ICO disclosed most of it but redacted the rest under section 40 (personal data), and withdrew its section 22 exemption during the investigation. The Commissioner found that the remaining redacted information is personal data and that disclosing it would be unlawful under Article 5(1)(a) and Article 6(1)(f) GDPR as applied through FOIA, so the withholding was appropriate and no further action was ordered. No fine was imposed.

The Slovenian DPA issued an advisory opinion on the establishment of a temporary information system for the combat against the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic to the government of the Republic of Slovenia and the Jozef Stefan Institute.

The IP issued the opinion that the police, when performing their tasks, may lawfully access video footage without the participants' consent, while any third party, such as an insurance company, should have an adequate legal basis under Article 6 GDPR to lawfully do so.

A complainant asked an insurance company to delete the health data he and his family gave in an insurance application, which he later withdrew from. The insurer refused, anonymised the records instead and said it was keeping them for five years to prevent insurance fraud. The Authority held that no GDPR ground justified refusing erasure or replacing erasure with anonymisation, so the insurer breached Articles 5 and 17 GDPR, and it issued a reprimand. It reserved judgment on the five-year retention practice until it examines the insurers' draft code of conduct under Article 40(5).

A dismissed employee complained that her employer had accessed the browsing history of her work PC, using a password shared with the company's legal representative, and used it in disciplinary proceedings ending in dismissal. The Garante found that the company gave no adequate prior information on monitoring, shared passwords contrary to security requirements, relied on a vague internal policy on internet checks, and only partly answered the access request without valid reasons. It ordered a restriction of the browsing-history data to storage for legal defence, compliance with the access request, security and policy changes, and fined the company EUR 10,000.
The AEPD fined mobile network operator Xfera Móviles, S.A.U. EUR. 5,000 because it failed to comply with the AEPD's order to provide all necessary information as required in Article 58(1) GDPR.

A data subject lodged a complaint against the Norwegian DPA alleging several GDPR violations. A third party was appointed to handle the case, since the DPA itself cannot handle complaints filed against it. The appointed representative held that the DPA violated Article 13 GDPR for failing to specify the legitimate interests for processing personal data on their website.

The Dutch DPA received a tip that CP&A, an inspection and maintenance company, kept an online sickness-absence register with health data of its employees. The register was a Google Drive file and it covered 25 sick employees. Between 12 March and 2 May 2019 the AP visited the web address known to it six times and found that it could view the register without any authentication or other access control. CP&A said the file could be reached only through a specific link, given to the people who handled sick leave and re-integration; the AP still found the security inadequate. The AP found a breach of the ban on processing health data (Art. 9(1) GDPR) and of the security obligation (Art. 32(1) GDPR). Policy rules produced base fines of EUR 725,000 and EUR 310,000 (EUR 1,035,000 together), but because CP&A's financial capacity is limited the AP reduced the total to EUR 15,000.

The Italian Data Protection Authority (Garante) delivered an opinion stating that the Udine City Council acted lawfully when providing for a limited civic access to the minutes of a district council meeting. The Garante considered the disclosure of the full handwritten minutes would have been unlawful, since violating the principles of purpose limitation and data minimization under Article 5(1)(b) and (c) GDPR.

The Information commission (the IP) issued an opinion explaining in which situation it is necessary for an employer to obtain information on employee’s sick leave for supervisory purposes, under Article 6(1)(c) GDPR.

The HDPA fined € 5.000 private centre for speech therapy because it did not fulfill the right of access exercised by a parent, who had the parental responsibility but not the custody, on behalf of his minor child. The controller also ignored HDPA's previous order to comply with the parent's request, thus violating Article 15(1) and (4) GDPR as well as the principle of accountability pursuant to Article 5(2) GDPR.

The Isle of Man Information Commissioner fined the Department of Home Affairs GBP 12,250 after a data subject complained that it had not properly answered a subject access request. The Department gave the data to the data subject piecemeal and took five months to supply it all, and only did so after the Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice in December 2019. The Commissioner also held that the Department had failed to comply with an earlier 2015 enforcement notice on the same subject. The Commissioner found the infringements negligent, not intentional, and treated the earlier enforcement action and the Department's representations downplaying its failure as aggravating. The Commissioner raised the penalty from the GBP 10,000 proposed in the Notice of Intent.

The Spanish data protection authority (AEPD) imposed a fine of 6,000 EUR on Oliveros Ustrell because the company could not prove the existence of consent for data processing activities, including the transfer of data to Vodafone.

A man who said he was assaulted at a bar asked the controller to freeze and later give him access to its camera footage, but received no proper answers, and the footage was deleted after 30 days without telling him. The Authority partly upheld his complaint, finding the controller failed to inform him properly about his restriction, access and footage requests, and ordered it to fulfil the access request. It also found, ex officio, a breach of the accountability principle in the camera surveillance. It fined the controller HUF 2,000,000 and rejected the complainant's own request for a fine.
The Garante issued a favorable opinion on the definition by Government decree of the channels (e.g. SMS, e-mail) through which electronic medical prescriptions shall be transmitted to patients.

The Slovenian Supervisory Authority (IP) issued an opinion as foreseen under Article 58(3) GDPR on the issue of the health data sharing under Article 9 GDPR in the employer - employee context. It held that there is no reason to collect such data by all organisations and companies, since in principle such information is provided through the National Institute of Public Health (NIJZ) epidemiological service. For all the other cases, the respective exceptions under Article 9(2) GDPR may apply.

The Slovenian Supervisory Authority (IP) issued an opinion as foreseen under Article 58(3) GDPR on the issue of the validity of consent to access digital content and online classrooms during the state of emergency in the Slovenia. The IP found that the consent may be given in writing, electronically or in another appropriate manner, and in any case should fulfill the requirements under Article 7 and Article 8 GDPR.

A complaint was lodged against Reykjavík Health Inspectorate, which during a waste inspection entered the complainant's private land without prior notice and took 23 photographs of property and vehicles, some with visible registration numbers. The Icelandic DPA found the processing was covered by the GDPR and rested on legal-obligation and public-authority grounds. It held the duty to inform under Articles 13 and 14 was not triggered and that the processing complied with the basic principles. The complaint was therefore not upheld, with no fine or order.

A data subject asked a debt collection agency to erase his personal data, which it refused, and disputed its practice of keeping settled collection files for six years. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman held that collection-related data may be kept for five years after the collection measures end, and that only data supporting accounting entries may be kept longer under the Bookkeeping Act. The controller was ordered to erase data linked to collection measures that ended five years earlier and that have no accounting entries. No fine was imposed.

The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) imposed a fine of 30,000 € on Telefónica Móviles España, S.AU. (the data controller) for infringing the obligation to comply with data subjects' requests to exercise their rights of access and erasure. The data controller had received an order with a previous AEPD's decision according to Article 58(2)(c) GDPR.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) imposed a fine of 5,000 € on a Centre for Studies, Centro de Estudios Dirigidos Delta, S.L. (the data controller), for the infringement of the principle of integrity and confidentiality, as per Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.
The AEPD fined EUR 4,000 individual for taking pictures at the beach without the consent of the data subjects.
The Croatian Personal Data Protection Agency (the AZOP) imposed a fine on a bank which failed to answer to a subject acess request and thus, infringed Article 15(3) GDPR.

An individual complained that Creditinfo Lánstraust hf. lowered his credit rating in a credit report between February 2017 and January 2018, although he had no arrears in that period. The rating was affected by a tax enforcement entry that had been removed from the company's arrears register after the debt was settled. The Authority held that using the deregistered entry had a legal basis under the legitimate-interests provision of Act No. 77/2000, was consistent with the operating licence, and raised no breach of the basic principles. It found the processing lawful and imposed no fine or order.

The Estonian Data Protection Authority (AKI) ruled on the removal of information from a criminal record. If a higher court does not amend or annul the conviction, the complainant has no right to request the rectification or deletion of the information from the criminal record.

The Danish Data Protection Authority reported Hørsholm Municipality to the police for insufficient security. A work computer holding personal data, including sensitive data and CPR numbers, of about 1,600 employees was stolen from an employee's car, and the computer was not encrypted. The authority proposed a fine of DKK 50,000. The Hørsholm municipality was later fined DKK 50,000 by the city court (byret). The same press release also covers Gladsaxe Municipality, which is not part of this record.

The Danish DPA reported Gladsaxe Municipality to the police and recommended DKK 100,000. The DPA’s page says the case is still before the courts, so no fine has been imposed. In Denmark the data protection authority cannot fine: it reports the case to the police and recommends an amount, and a court sets the fine.

The Swedish DPA (Datainspektionen) imposed a fine of 75 million Swedish kronor (approximately € 7 million) on Google for failing to fulfill its obligation in respect of the right to be forgotten (Article 17 GDPR).

The Estonian Data Protection Authority (AKI) confirmed that the police are not entitled to deny access to requested documents, if the applicable national law only foresees restrictions for a limited time period that is exceeded and no other legal ground for an access restriction applies.

The Polish DPA planned an inspection of a company that supplied the IT system used by a telemarketing firm, because that firm had no access to the personal data processed in the system. The company gave notice ending the lease of its registered address (a virtual office) two days before the inspection, and no representative was present at the address on either inspection day. It was then put into liquidation. The President of the UODO found a breach of Article 31 in conjunction with Article 58(1)(e) and (f) GDPR (failure to cooperate and to give access to data and premises) and imposed a fine of PLN 20,000.

A debt collector recorded the phone number of the complainant, who only acted as a contact for a relative's debtor file, as the debtor's number. It then sent debt-collection SMS messages to that number, and it could not show that the complainant had consented. The authority found breaches of the accuracy principle (Art. 5(1)(d)) and of the lawful-basis rule (Art. 6(1)), and fined the company HUF 300,000. It rejected the complaint about the home address and e-mail address, found no breach of the access/erasure provisions, and discontinued the part about ordering erasure because the number had already been deleted. The authority also paid the complainant HUF 10,000 for exceeding its own procedural deadline.

BroBizz A/S, a Danish road-toll payment company, notified three personal data breaches in 2019. In each case customer service staff disclosed customer data, including location data, to unauthorised people, such as an ex-partner. Datatilsynet found that BroBizz's risk assessment and organisational measures for verifying identity under data subject requests were inadequate, and issued serious criticism under Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It also ordered BroBizz to carry out a risk assessment within 4 weeks, and found the breach notifications under Articles 33(1) and 34(1) compliant.

A former employee of the addiction treatment organisation SÁÁ received a box of patient records when he was handed his personal belongings after leaving in 2018. The records included registration books with names of about 3,000 patients and detailed medical records of 252 people. Persónuvernd found that the disclosure resulted from insufficient technical and organisational security measures. It imposed an administrative fine of ISK 3,000,000, taking into account the sensitive data and the non-profit, public-benefit nature of the organisation and its ongoing compliance work.

The municipality published on its website, in its public register and in a separate section, a determination appointing a lawyer, together with the full citation summons that a complainant had filed against the municipality. The documents exposed the complainant's personal data, including name, birth details, address, tax code and a detailed account of his personal, professional and judicial history. The Garante found that the publication had no adequate legal basis and that naming the complainant in the determination breached the data minimisation principle. It imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website. The data were removed by September 2018.

The IP issues an opinion on the lawful installation and operation of video-surveillance systems. It stresses that the operators are the data controllers and the ones who must be able to prove the lawfulness of the system. According to national law, if the system is to be installed in an apartment complex, all owners of property must give their consent.

Persónuvernd imposed a fine of 1 300 000 ISK (approx. 9000 euro) on Fjölbrautaskólinn í Breiðholti (FB) for lacking technical and organisational measures and being in breach of Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR. The security breach took place when a teacher mistakenly attached a document, which included special categories of data from earlier interviews, in an email to new students at the school.

The Icelandic DPA decided that the electronic complaint form on the webpage of the Citizens' Ombudsman violated Articles 5 (1)(f) and 32 GDPR. The use of HTTPS protocols must be used to minimise the risk of unauthorized access to information shared through websites.

The Estonian Data Protection Authority (AKI) emphasized that an existing legal basis for the publication of personal data does not entitle to re-use and disclose the published information for any purpose.

The Commissioner examined a personal data breach notified by Hellenic Bank. Because two customers had been recorded under the same passport number, one customer could see card and account details of another customer in web banking, and a card was sent to the wrong address. The Commissioner found infringements of Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1)(b) and 33(1) GDPR. She decided not to impose a fine, because mitigating factors clearly outweighed aggravating ones, and instead ordered the bank to adopt security measures and report on compliance within three months.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) decided to impose a fine up to 60,000 € on Vodafone España, S.AU. (the data controller) for the infringement of the lawfulness of processing principle, as per Article 6(1) GDPR.

A former chair of a company board complained that a local councillor and deputy mayor posted on his official Facebook page a photo of the complainant, with his minor child, without consent. The Authority found the photo was taken and published without a legal basis and in breach of lawfulness, purpose limitation and data minimisation. It also found the respondent ignored the complainant's access and erasure requests. It reprimanded him, banned the processing, ordered deletion of the photo, ordered publication of the decision with his identity, and fined him HUF 100,000 on its own initiative. The complainant's own request for a fine was rejected because he is not a party on that point.

Scottish company was fined £500,000 for making more than 193 million automated nuisance calls. The ICO found that people who received the calls had not given their consent, had not been provided with a valid opt-out option and couldn't identify who was making the calls. This way the company violated Section 40 of the Data Protection Act 1998 and Regulations 19 and 24 of Privacy and Electronic Communication Regulations 2003.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) decided to impose a fine EUR 48,000 on Vodafone Ono, S.A.U. as data controller for the infringement of the security of processing principle, as per Article 32 GDPR.
Following an investigation, the Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) imposed a fine of 120,000 Eur on VODAFONE ESPAÑA SAU (Vodafone) for a serious violation of Articles 6(1)(a) and 5(1)(a) GDPR.

The Romanian authority completed an investigation into Dante Internațional S.A., the operator of e-MAG.ro, on 27 February 2020. It found the company sent a commercial email to a private individual at the end of 2019, although it had confirmed that person's unsubscription from commercial communications at the start of 2019. The company was fined 14,420.4 lei, stated as the equivalent of EUR 3,000, under Article 6 GDPR read with Article 21(3). The authority also ordered it to deactivate the individual's marketing email setting within 3 working days and to ensure compliance with Article 21 within 20 days.

Datatilsynet carried out a planned inspection of Udbetaling Danmark in 2019, focusing on how it handles access requests. It found that in five access cases the authority did not tell the data subject that automated decisions had been made about them (Article 15(1)(h)). It also found that in three cases, plus one case caused by a misunderstanding, access requests were not answered within the one-month deadline (Article 12(3)). Datatilsynet expressed criticism without imposing a fine and recommended clarifying its guidelines and templates.

BEC, a shared IT centre that processed automatic payment transfers for Danish banks, sent address details of people registered in the CPR with protected or omitted addresses to payees, through faults in its systems. More than 20,000 customers were affected, and banks reported the breaches to Datatilsynet, which then opened its own investigation. Datatilsynet found that BEC had not met the requirements of Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32(1) GDPR and issued a severe criticism (alvorlig kritik). No fine is stated in the decision.

A former board member of a Glyfada municipal golf company complained that the company did not answer his access requests for CCTV footage showing him, sent by email, fax and letter. The company claimed the recorder was out of order, but the Authority found this was not proven and that no reply was given within the deadline. The Authority found a breach of the access right in the (pre-GDPR) Law 2472/1997 and imposed a fine of EUR 5,000.

A woman complained that her brother's extended reliability check by the military Defence Department (Abwehramt) involved disclosing her home address without her knowledge, breaching her rights to secrecy and information. The authority found that her data was only held in a paper bundle that could not easily be retrieved, so it was not a filing system under the DSG and the information duties did not apply, and no data protection right was breached. The complaint was dismissed, and no fine was imposed.

The Norwegian DPA initially notified the Public Roads Administration of a NOK 4 million fine for failing to delete toll road crossing logs, thus violating Article 5(1) GDPR, Article 17(1)(a), Article 17(1)(d) and Article 25(1), cf. Article 5(1)(c), Article 5(1)(d), Article 5(1)(e) and Article 5(1)(f). The controller, however, contested the decision, leading the DPA to reassess the case and subsequently reduce the fine to NOK 1 million (approximately €98,000 in June 2021).

The AEPD fined 48 000 € a Spanish hospital group for the violation of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1)(a) GDPR, and thus, for the processing of personal data without any legal basis. The AEPD ruled that the data controller obtained the data subject's consent for the sharing of personal data to third parties through "opt-out" clause.

The Romanian supervisory authority investigated Enel Energie Muntenia SA after a customer complained. The company had emailed one customer's personal data (name, address, email, customer code and account code) to another customer. The authority found a breach of Article 32 GDPR because the company had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures. It imposed a fine equivalent to EUR 3,000 and ordered the company to bring its security measures into compliance within 30 working days.
Under Austrian procedural law a successful complainant is not a party to the penal procedure, when a penalty under the GDPR is imposed.

A complainant asked the utility DEH for copies of all her physical and electronic correspondence with it from 2015 onward and received no reply. DEH later told the Authority that no such correspondence existed, and that power had been cut at the request of the supplier over unpaid arrears. The Authority found that DEH, as controller, did not reply within one month or inform the complainant of the reason for the delay, in breach of Article 12(3) and (4) GDPR. Because DEH had committed the same breach in an earlier decision (15/2019), the Authority imposed a fine of EUR 5,000.

A individual who received a sales call from an electricity retailer asked the company where it had obtained his current electricity supplier and what other data it held on him. The sales call had been recorded, and the company did not provide the recording or the requested data, instead offering only to let him listen to it on its premises or by phone. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found that the company had not fulfilled the access right under Article 15 GDPR, and that its call-recording information practice was not transparent enough under Articles 5(1)(a), 12(1) and 13. The decision ordered compliance with the access request, a change of practice for access to call recordings and for recording notices, and issued a reprimand. No fine was imposed.
The AEPD fined €1,500 a data controller for the lack of a privacy policy on its website, under Article 13 GDPR.

The President of the Personal Data Protection Office of Poland (PUODO) imposed a fine of €4,700 (PLN 20,000) on a primary school for unlawful processing of children's biometric data when using the school canteen.

KMD A/S, acting as a processor, took over a development and test server from another supplier after an acquisition. The server was connected to the internet, was not covered by KMD's normal security set-up, and was not assessed for personal data. In April 2019 it was compromised and used to mine Bitcoin, and it turned out to hold personal data for 68 controllers, mainly municipalities. Datatilsynet found that basic technical measures such as firewall rules would have prevented the breach, and it expressed criticism of KMD for insufficient security under Article 32 GDPR. No fine was imposed.

The Romanian supervisory authority was notified that an association, SOS Infertilitatea, had disclosed personal data without the data subject's consent. It asked the association for information but received no reply, even after a phone call in which the association's president asked for the request to be sent by email. The authority concluded its investigation on 13 February 2020 and found the association had not provided the requested information under Art. 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR. It fined the association 9,529.2 lei (about EUR 2,000) under Art. 83(5)(e) and ordered it to send all requested information in writing within 5 working days.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation at Vodafone România SA on 13 February 2020, following a complaint from a woman who asked for an offer through the operator's website and then received by email a contract concluded with another individual. The authority found breaches of Law 506/2004 (security of processing and failure to notify a breach), not the GDPR. Vodafone received two contravention fines totalling 20,000 lei and was recommended to implement adequate security measures within 30 days and to notify security breaches without delay in future.

A municipal employee complained that the Comune di Urago d'Oglio had published on its website a document and the full text of a court judgment containing her personal data, including health data. The Garante found there was no legal basis for the publication, that it breached the principles of lawfulness and minimisation, and that it violated the ban on disseminating health data. The municipality's arguments (implicit consent, Article 52 of the Code, transparency) were rejected. The Garante imposed a fine of EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website; no corrective measures were needed since the data had been removed.
On 14 February the Informacijski pooblaščenec of the Republic of Slovenia (IP), provided a non-binding opinion pursuant to Article 58(3) GDPR. The IP pronounced itself on the use of drones.

The Informacijski pooblaščenec, Information Commissioner of the Republic of Slovenia (IP), provided an opinion pursuant to Article 58 GDPR. The subject matter of the opinion regarded processing of personal data in an employment context.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued a non-binding opinion regarding the processing of data in the context of a life insurance policy. It recalled several provisions of the Slovenian Insurance Act (ZZavar) and found that insurance companies may have a proper legal basis for the processing of personal data in specific databases if the companies fulfill the requirements provided for in ZZavar. It also noted that in the context of a non-binding opinion the IP cannot determine whether in a particular case these requirements are fulfilled.

On 14 February the Informacijski pooblaščenec, Information Commissioner of the Republic of Slovenia (IP), provided a non-binding opinion pursuant to Article 58 GDPR. The subject matter of the opinion regarded the legality of installing an automatic camera for the purpose of monitoring recreational activities on watercourses in the Triglay National Park (TNP). The IP refrained from commenting in the particular, but highlighted areas which required a closer look by the park.

A complainant objected to the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI) showing banner ads on its website, which passed visitors' personal data, including cookie identifiers and IP addresses, to Google without a valid legal basis. DMI admitted that data had been collected and passed on without legal basis for visitors who had opted out of cookies, and it changed its consent solution during the case. The Danish DPA found that neither the earlier nor the current consent solution met the GDPR consent requirements or the principle of lawfulness, fairness and transparency, and that the processing lacked a legal basis under Article 6. It issued a serious criticism (reprimand) and imposed no fine.

The Romanian authority completed an investigation into Vodafone România SA and found it had mishandled a natural person's personal data while handling that person's complaint. The controller's reply was sent to an incorrect email address because insufficient security measures were in place. The authority imposed a fine of 14,308.8 lei (about EUR 3,000) and ordered the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures, including regular staff training, within 30 days of the minutes being communicated.

The ICO issued Cathay Pacific Airways Limited with a monetary penalty under the Data Protection Act 1998 for a serious contravention of the seventh data protection principle (data security). A breach that had run from at least October 2014 to May 2018 exposed personal data of about 9.4 million data subjects, including passport numbers. The ICO found a series of security failings, including unencrypted backups, unpatched systems, missing multi-factor authentication and excessive administrator privileges, and found the contraventions negligent. It also found a breach of the fifth principle on retention. The penalty was £500,000, reducible to £400,000 for payment by 12 March 2020.

A teacher complained that the art high school in Naples had published on its website an old school ranking list of teaching staff containing excessive personal data, including tax codes, addresses, phone numbers, emails, and a code revealing disability status for about 25 teachers. The Garante found the publication unlawful under data minimisation, lawfulness and the ban on disseminating health data. It imposed a fine of EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website. No corrective measures were ordered because the list had already been removed.

A woman complained about a segment of the TV programme 'Le Iene' in which she was interviewed, face obscured, by someone posing as a client, and her real voice and personal details were broadcast and put online, making her identifiable. The Garante found the processing unlawful as it breached the fairness and lawfulness principle and the journalistic code of conduct, including the rules on sexual-sphere data. It fined RTI EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The video had already been removed during the investigation, and the claim for compensation was held to be outside its competence.

On 6 February 2020, ICO adopted a decision, stating that the Northamptonshire Police acted lawfully by refusing to confirm or deny whether it held information requested by the complainant. However, ICO found that the Northamptonshire Police’s failure to specify the exemption on which it was relying constituted a breach. These conclusions were made based on the relevant provisions of the Freedom of Information Act 2000 ("FOIA"), Data Protection Act 2018 and the General Data Protection regulation ("GDPR").

The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) decided not to take further actions over the Department for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport (DCMS) for its management of a UK citizen's (the complainant) request of information on which articles of the (now repealed) Directive 95/46/EC, according to the European Commission, had not been properly implemented by the UK government at the (now repealed) Data Protection Act 1998.
Luxembourg DPA argues it cannot proceed and is not willing to open an investigation against a company established abroad that has not designated an EU Represenative.
The AEPD imposed a 1.500 € fine against a cafeteria which placed surveillance cameras outside its establishment on a public space and thus, violated the principle of data minimisation.
Following an investigation the Spanish Data Protection Authority imposed a fine of EUR 60,000 on XFERA MÓVILES for violation of Article 6(1)(a) GDPR.

A woman complained to the AEPD that Vodafone España billed her for a phone line she says she never contracted, and Vodafone did not answer the Agency's information requests. The AEPD opened a sanction procedure for processing her data without a legal basis (Article 6.1 GDPR) and proposed a fine of EUR 100,000. Vodafone paid EUR 60,000 on 24 December 2019, using both 20% reductions (acknowledging responsibility and voluntary payment). The AEPD therefore closed the procedure under Article 85 of Law 39/2015.

Following an investigation the AEPD imposed a fine of 20.000 EUR on IBERIA Airlines for the violation of Article 6(1)(f) GDPR, when further sending unsolicited emails after a customer has requested the deletion of his data.

The Spanish AEPD closed proceedings PS/00292/2019 after the respondent paid voluntarily. The respondent had posted a fake adult-contact advert on a website using the complainant's photo, name, phone number and sexual descriptions, created from an IP address linked to a company. The proposed fine was EUR 1,000 for infringing Article 6(1) GDPR; a 20% reduction for voluntary payment brought it to EUR 800, which was paid on 16 January 2020. The payment waived administrative appeals.

The ICO decided that Devon and Cornwall Police rightly refused to disclose information about the death of a man with mental health issues who had been restrained with an emergency response belt while in police custody. It considered the information personal data and it found that disclosure would be generally unlawful, since the admitted legal basis of legitimate interest is not sufficient to outweigh the data subject’s fundamental rights and freedoms.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued a non-binding opinion as foreseen under Article 58(3) GDPR regarding spamming e-mails to Slovenian company, which were sent by a travel agency without any prior registration.

The Estonian Data Protection Authority (AKI) ruled that the access to public information may be lawfully restricted when the documents requested are not finalised. A non signed environmental impact assessment drafted by the Ministry of Environment falls under this restriction.

On the 31st January 2020 the Information Commissioners Office (ICO) supported the position of the City of York Council, finding that details of the Council's employees professional qualifications amounted to personal information. As such, the City of York Council were correct in applying the Section 40(2) Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA) exemption.

A teacher complained that the Nobel secondary school in Torre del Greco had published on its website the school's teacher ranking lists, with home addresses, phone numbers and other personal data. The Garante found the lists were fully downloadable and contained data on over 2,000 teachers, including unnecessary details such as tax codes and emails, and a code revealing the disability status of about 20 teachers. It held that this breached the lawfulness and data minimisation principles, lacked a legal basis for publication and breached the ban on disseminating health data. It fined the school EUR 4,000, ordered publication of the decision, and imposed no corrective measures since the document had already been removed.

A private individual reported to the Garante that the municipality of Colledara had published on its website full lists and records of a public recruitment competition, including names, birth data, scores and oral exam questions of candidates, including those excluded or not successful. The municipality removed the documents and argued that the call for applications and candidates' acceptance of it justified publication. The Garante held that no law or regulation provided a legal basis for such dissemination, that consent cannot serve as a basis for public bodies, and that the principles of lawfulness and data minimisation were breached. It fined the municipality EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website; no corrective measures were imposed since the conduct had ceased.

A private person found a printed list in their garden containing about 100 people's tax IDs, social security numbers, birth data and unencrypted Client Gate (government portal) usernames and passwords. It turned out to belong to an accounting firm, which kept the credentials file on paper as well as on its server. The authority opened proceedings of its own motion and found the firm had not applied adequate security measures (Art. 32(1) GDPR). It also found that the firm's incident-handling policy did not cover notifying the supervisory authority (Art. 24(1)-(2) GDPR). It ordered the firm to stop keeping the database on paper and to amend its policy, and fined it HUF 500,000.

A hospital in Verona notified the Garante of three personal data breaches found in its own periodic audits: staff had improperly accessed the electronic health records (dossier sanitario) of 16 patients who were also hospital colleagues, out of curiosity, and in some cases by using a colleague's unattended logged-in workstation. The Garante found that the hospital's technical and organisational measures did not adequately limit access to treating staff, in breach of Art. 5(1)(f) GDPR. It ordered the hospital to complete the access-control measures within 90 days and fined it EUR 30,000. The decision is to be published in full on the Garante's website.

On December 2020, 23rd the Italian Data Protection Authority imposed a fine of 30 000 Euro on the university of Rome “la Sapienza”, acting as a data controller under the GDPR. The data controller did not process personal data with an appropriate level of security, as required by article 32, read in conjunction with article 33 GDPR.

With the provision No. 10 of 23 january 2020, the Italian Data Protection Authority assessed Istat's request for authorization to process data, pursuant to article 2-quinquiesdecies of the Privacy Code (Legislative Decree 196/2003).

The Garante received several hundred complaints and reports about unwanted promotional calls made for TIM, and TIM also sent a series of data breach notifications. After inspections at TIM and at its marketing partners, it found many violations in TIM's marketing: calls without consent, poorly managed opt-out lists, objections to marketing not respected, forced consent in the TIM Party programme and in apps and paper forms, long retention of data of other operators' customers, and poor breach and data-accuracy management. It imposed a single fine of EUR 27,802,946, set at 0.2% of TIM's turnover. It also ordered a permanent restriction of certain processing, a series of corrective measures and publication of the decision.

A man complained that the municipality of Francavilla Fontana had published on its online official notice board a determination on legal costs that contained details of his health conditions linked to service, and the full IBAN of a lawyer. The Garante found the publication unlawful, as health data may not be disseminated and the IBAN went beyond what was necessary. The municipality had said it was a clerical error, had removed the document and described measures taken. It did not reply to the notice of violations. The Garante fined the municipality EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Commissioner's web page for October to December 2019 summarises a case about a leak of personal data from the Social Insurance Services' computerised system, after press reports in August 2017. Two staff members accessed citizens' data with their own passwords, printed screenshots and gave them to a retired police officer, and the Services gave incomplete answers to the Commissioner and had inadequate security measures at the time. The Commissioner found a breach of Article 32(1)(b) and (d) and 32(4) GDPR and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 9,000. The page does not give the decision's own date.

A complainant received an unsolicited promotional SMS from eShop for Sports (M.L. PRO.FIT SOLUTIONS LTD) without a free way to stop the messages, although she had already complained about the same controller. The controller said her number had been removed but that its messaging provider's system had failed for technical reasons, and that the provider had no free opt-out number. Taking mitigating factors into account, including that no other data subject had complained to the Commissioner about this controller, a fine of EUR 1,000 was imposed. The text is a summary page covering several decisions from October to December 2019 and does not name the articles breached for this case.

A former employee of the company complained that, after his departure, the company had searched its server and his work computer, removed a hard drive, and kept his personal data without informing him or giving him access. The Authority found a breach of the principles of Article 5 GDPR (Article 5(1)(a) and 5(2) are the ones named in the operative part) and ordered the company to answer the access request, to bring its video surveillance processing into line with the GDPR, and to fix its compliance with Article 5. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 15,000.

The Estonian DPA (AKI) ruled that any settlement of claims between data controller and data subject does not deprive the latter of the possibility to exercise their right of access according to Article 15 GDPR, regardless of the fact that the data controller is a public or private entity.
Vodafone has been fined € 44.000 for accidentally disclosing personal data to a third party.

A man received a garnishment notice from a private bailiff in an enforcement case against a third party with the same three names. The utility company had supplied his personal identification number (ЕГН) to the bailiff, which was wrong, and the garnishment was later lifted. The Commission found the utility company had processed his name and ID number without any legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR. It imposed a fine of 10,000 BGN, close to the minimum. The complaint against the bailiff was dismissed, as the Commission found the bailiff's processing lawful.

The Saarland annual report for 2020 describes fine proceedings against police officers who looked up personal data in police databases for purely private reasons, mostly concerning colleagues or superiors. Because the officers decided the purposes themselves, they were treated as controllers under the GDPR, and the queries were treated as violations of Articles 5 and 6. Given the special trust placed in the police, fines were imposed in each case under Article 83(5), in the low to mid three-digit range. The report gives no exact amounts, officers' names or dates, and recommends regular training and spot checks of query logs.

The annual report describes a case of 'employee excess' at a company that runs a COVID-19 testing centre. After a test, an employee used a young woman's data to contact her privately via WhatsApp and get to know her. The woman filed a criminal complaint and the prosecutor passed the case to the Hessian authority. The authority held that the employee acted purely for private purposes and so was himself responsible, and fined him EUR 300 under Art. 83(5)(a) in conjunction with Art. 5(1)(b) GDPR. The fine notice was not yet final when the report was written.

The annual report describes a case in which a ballet school operator published photos of minor pupils on her website and Facebook page. A father complained that photos of his minor daughter were online without his permission. The operator could not prove that valid consents existed for past publications. The case went to the fine office, which imposed three fines. Two were for single images of the complainant's daughter (Art. 6(1)). One was for missing written documentation of lawfulness for the other pupils' photos (Art. 5(1),(2) and Art. 7(1)). Together the fines came to a four-figure amount, and the operator accepted them.

A medical assistant at a Brandenburg doctor's practice saved a patient's telephone number, which was held for treatment purposes, in her mobile phone and contacted him privately. The patient had not consented, and he complained to the authority. The authority opened administrative fine proceedings against the assistant for unlawful processing under Art. 6(1) GDPR. It imposed a fine in the three-figure range. The report gives no exact amount.

The Hessian data protection authority received several complaints against a small capital company based in Hesse about access requests under Article 15 GDPR. After two of these complaints were examined and violations found, it opened a fine procedure. The company missed the deadline for answering two access requests, and in one case the data had been deleted before the access could be given. The authority imposed one fine notice for both violations, in the mid five-figure range; the report says the fine is not yet final.

The Hamburg data protection authority's 2020 annual report describes a fine against a company that runs an online marketplace for worn underwear. Photos uploaded by users still carried location metadata (GPS/EXIF data), because a misconfigured add-on of the content management system did not strip it. About 760 women were affected, and a citizen's tip led to the fine proceedings. The report calls the fine low because of the company's small turnover but gives no amount. The company did not appeal and paid, and it fixed the fault.

Several companies of one corporate group, all offering adult education courses, kept a shared customer database. A person who owed fees to one of them was turned away by another company in the group because of his payment arrears. After his complaint, the Hamburg authority found that the companies were joint controllers, which requires an agreement under Art. 26 GDPR. No such agreement existed, so the authority imposed a fine of EUR 13,000. The report is an annual report, and this case is one short section within it.

The 2020 annual report of the Lower Saxony data protection authority describes a fine on the operator of an online shop. After a breach notification, the authority checked the website and found it ran an outdated web-shop application. The version had been outdated since 2014 at the latest and no longer received security updates from the vendor; it allowed SQL injection attacks. The authority found a breach of Art. 32(1) GDPR and fined the company EUR 65,500, which the company accepted. In setting the amount it took into account that the company had told affected people to change their passwords before the fine proceedings began.

A Bangladeshi national asked the Authority to have his data deleted from the National Register of Undesirable Aliens (EKANA), after the Attica Aliens Directorate had refused his deletion requests. He had been registered after being arrested without residence documents, having a criminal conviction, and a pending return decision. The Authority held that the registration was lawful on public order and security grounds, that the three-year review period had not yet run, and dismissed the complaint as unfounded. No fine was imposed.

A complainant who had registered an objection to marketing use of his name with the Icelandic national register (Þjóðskrá Íslands) received a marketing email from Síminn hf. The company argued that Act No 81/2003 on electronic communications, which allows opt-out at the start and in each email, overrode the data protection act. The Authority held that the data protection act's register-checking duty applies and is not displaced, so the company had to check its mailing list against the register before sending. Because it did not, the sending of the marketing email did not comply with the law; no fine is stated in the text.

A list of sick-leave absences of staff in a hotel kitchen owned by Íslandshótel hf. was posted for a time in a room accessible to all hotel staff. Two employees, who were the complainants, complained through their union. The Data Protection Authority found that the company had not ensured adequate security for this health-related data, as required by the Icelandic act implementing Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, so the processing did not comply with the law. No fine was imposed; the company was ordered to adopt staff data-handling procedures, make them available to all staff and present them to managers, and confirm compliance by 27 January 2020.

A Greek group company, Aegean Bunkering Services, notified a data breach and reported that people linked to Aegean Marine Petroleum Network Inc (AMPNI) and an audit firm had entered its data room and copied a whole server, including staff emails and the data of employees of unrelated third-party companies. The authority issued interim orders banning any processing of the copied data and later heard the companies and the complainants. It found that AMPNI had infringed the data protection principles and the lawfulness requirement (Articles 5 and 6(1) GDPR), including the security principle. It ordered AMPNI to bring its processing into line within three months, covering the original servers and the copy sent to Manchester, and imposed a fine of EUR 150,000. In setting the fine it took into account AMPNI's bankruptcy filing in the US and its reported revenue.

A city councillor complained that a local party posted on its public Facebook page the attendance list of a non-public meeting, with a comment that he had not attended, and that this breached his right to confidentiality. The authority held that the media privilege in §9 DSG did not apply, that the party was controller under Art. 4(7) GDPR, and that the balancing of the party's freedom of expression against the councillor's interest in confidentiality favoured the party. The complaint was dismissed, and the decision is final.

Nemlig.com A/S reported a personal data breach in January 2019. A web-based report service had no adequate access control, so customer order details (name, address, customer number, order contents) could be reached online for about 250,000 customers. Nemlig decided not to notify the data subjects, but the Danish Data Protection Agency found that the risk to customers with secret or omitted addresses had not been assessed and was high. The agency ordered Nemlig to notify the affected data subjects who may have a secret or omitted address, or all affected customers if those cannot be identified.

Intervare A/S reported a personal data breach in January 2019. A web-based report service without adequate access control exposed order data (name, address, customer number and order contents) of about 16,000 Intervare customers on the internet. Intervare decided not to notify the data subjects. The Danish Data Protection Agency found that no proper Article 34(1) risk assessment had been made, in particular regarding customers with secret or unlisted addresses, and ordered Intervare to notify the affected data subjects.

A complainant who used the nursing care services of a non-profit organisation (a VZW) that the decision calls Y sent it a subject access request under Article 15 GDPR and later a request for erasure, and received no response within one month. The Litigation Chamber found that the controller failed to respond to the access and erasure requests within the time limit of Article 12(3) and failed to provide the information under Article 15. It ordered the organisation to comply with the access and erasure requests within 20 working days and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 for the breaches of Articles 12.3 and 15.

The Litigation Chamber of the Belgian DPA fined the operator of a legal news website EUR 15,000. The DPA's inspection service found that the privacy policy omitted the controller's identity, purposes, legal basis, retention periods and data subject rights, and that the cookie banner used pre-ticked boxes, had no reject option and relied on a 'legitimate interest' basis for analytics cookies that required consent. The chamber found breaches of Articles 6, 7 (with 4(11)), 12 and 13 GDPR. It noted that later improvements did not cancel the original breaches and ordered publication of the decision without naming the controller.

The Romanian authority concluded an investigation of an energy supplier on 16 December 2019. It found that the company processed a complainant's data unlawfully, being unable to prove consent to send notifications to his email address, and without respecting accuracy. The company also did not stop the notifications although the complainant objected several times. Two administrative fines of 14,334.30 lei each (about EUR 3,000 each) were imposed, and the company has paid them.

The Swedish DPA examined Nusvar AB, which ran the people-search website mrkoll.se and resold Yellow-Belly credit reports from December 2018 to 8 April 2019. The site published payment-remark information derived from neighbourhood clusters and information that individuals had been charged in criminal cases, for over eight million people. The DPA found breaches of Article 10 GDPR and section 6 of the Credit Information Act (criminal offence data without permission), Article 5 GDPR (excessive data), and sections 9 and 11 of the Credit Information Act (legitimate need and credit report copy). It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 35,000, and no further corrective measure because the credit reporting had ceased.

Romania's data protection authority concluded an investigation on 13 December 2019 into a shipping and trading company, following a complaint about audio-video cameras in offices and changing rooms, fingerprint access control, and use of a former employee's identity in work emails. It found four sets of infringements. It issued two warnings (for failing to inform data subjects, and for unlawfully using a former employee's data in emails) and two fines of RON 23,893 (about EUR 5,000) each, for excessive video surveillance of employees and for processing biometric fingerprint data when less intrusive means were available. It also ordered corrective measures on information, data minimisation in video monitoring and access control, and security policies.

Following a complaint, the Romanian DPA investigated a company and closed the investigation on 13 December 2019. It found excessive video surveillance of employees in offices and changing areas, processing of employees' fingerprints, inadequate information to data subjects, and unlawful use of a former employee's data in emails. It issued two fines of RON 23,893 (EUR 5,000 each) and two warnings, plus corrective measures on transparency, data minimisation and security.

A former employee asked his ex-employer three times in June and July 2019 for access to his personal data under Article 15 GDPR and received no reply. After the Office warned the company in October 2019, it sent a data dump that lacked required information and covered only the last 30 days, withholding data citing third-party rights and trade secrets. The Office issued a penalty order finding an offence for breaching the right of access and imposed a fine of CZK 50,000, at the very bottom of the range, noting the company did not remedy the situation even after the warning.

A former hospital director complained that the hospital's successor institution kept archived copies of his work e-mail accounts, which he had been allowed to use privately, and searched them for a document without telling him. The authority upheld the complaint. It found breaches of storage limitation, fairness, purpose limitation and lawful basis. It also found, of its own motion, a breach of accountability and transparency. It banned storage of the private correspondence, ordered a review and deletion, and ordered internal rules and information for staff on e-mail archiving and searches. It fined the institution HUF 500,000 and ordered the authority to pay the complainant HUF 10,000 for exceeding the processing deadline.

The Garante investigated Eni Gas e Luce after dozens of complaints about promotional calls made without consent, after opt-outs, or to numbers on the public opposition register. An inspection in February 2019 showed systemic problems in the company's telemarketing and teleselling: no checks on consent in lists bought from list providers, consent refusals not respected, late updating of blacklists, over-long data retention, and poor cooperation with the authority. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, imposed corrective orders and a fine of EUR 8,500,000, set at 5% of the statutory maximum of EUR 171.16 million, and ordered publication of the decision.

Several people complained to the Italian DPA that Eni Gas e Luce had signed energy supply contracts they never requested, often with wrong personal data, through door-to-door sales agencies. After inspections in February 2019, the Garante found that Eni's organisational and technical controls over its agencies were inadequate, so inaccurate data were processed (about 7,200 customers affected) in breach of the fairness, accuracy, integrity and accountability principles. It ordered Eni to bring its processes into line within six months, permanently restricted further processing of the data of the 7,200 customers, and fined it EUR 3,000,000, with publication of the decision.
The HDPA issued a reprimand to the Ministry of Mercantile Marine and Island Policy for infringement of the right of access.

After a complaint that Hora Credit IFN SA had sent e-mails containing another person's personal data, and kept doing so after the error was reported, the Romanian authority found breaches of the principles in Article 5, the security duties in Articles 25 and 32, and the breach notification duty in Article 33. Three fines were imposed, in lei with euro equivalents of EUR 3,000, EUR 10,000 and EUR 1,000. The authority also ordered corrective measures on email data validation, secure transmission and breach-notification policy, with 30-day deadlines.

The German Federal Data Protection Commissioner fined the telecom provider 1&1 Telecom GmbH EUR 9,550,000. Callers to its customer service could obtain extensive customer data just by giving a customer's name and date of birth. The BfDI saw this authentication procedure as a breach of Article 32 GDPR. Because the company cooperated throughout the proceedings, the BfDI set the fine in the lower part of the possible range. The company also tightened its authentication and is introducing a new procedure. The BfDI held that a fine was still called for despite these measures. The press release also announces a separate EUR 10,000 fine against Rapidata GmbH, which is not part of this record.

A BfDI press release announces two fines. This record concerns the smaller one: Rapidata GmbH, a telecoms provider, was fined EUR 10,000 because it failed to appoint a data protection officer despite being asked several times. The amount took into account that the company is a micro-enterprise. The same press release also covers a EUR 9,550,000 fine against 1&1 Telecom GmbH under Article 32, which is not part of this record.

The Dutch DPA received a tip in July 2018 that a company obliged its employees to scan their fingerprints to clock in and out. After an ex officio investigation with unannounced visits in November 2018 and March 2019, it found that the company processed employees' biometric data from 25 May 2018 to 16 April 2019 without a valid exception under Article 9(2) GDPR (neither explicit consent nor the UAVG authentication/security exception). It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 725,000, which is the base fine of category IV under its 2019 fine policy rules, with no increase or decrease. It rejected the company's arguments that a reprimand would suffice and that it relied on its supplier.

The Rhineland-Palatinate data protection commissioner fined a hospital in the state EUR 105,000. The fine followed a patient mix-up at admission, which led to an incorrect invoice and revealed structural technical and organisational shortcomings in the hospital's patient management. The press release says the fine is final and that the authority welcomes the hospital's substantiated efforts to improve its data protection management. The commissioner stresses that the main aim is to remedy deficits and that the fine is also a signal of particular vigilance in health data protection.

The Romanian data protection authority ANSPDCP sanctioned Nicola Medical Team 17 SRL on 2 December 2019 for not providing information the authority had requested. The company first received a warning and an order to supply the information within 10 calendar days. Because it did not comply, it was fined RON 9,555.4 (stated as EUR 2,000) and given a further order to provide the information within 5 days. The text is a news page covering two decisions; only item 2 concerns this decision.

The authority completed an investigation on 29 November 2019 into a homeowners association after a complainant alleged that images from the association's video surveillance system were accessed, used and disclosed to various people without legal basis. The investigation found the association had not adopted sufficient technical and organisational security measures to protect the CCTV data. The association was fined the equivalent of EUR 500 (RON 2,389.05) and received two warnings, plus corrective orders on informing data subjects and on security measures.

The Romanian authority, using its investigative powers, sanctioned Modern Barber S.R.L. on 26 November 2019 for failing to provide information it had requested (GDPR Art. 58(1)(a) and (e)). It first issued a warning and ordered the company to supply the information within 10 days. When the company did not comply, it was fined 14,329.5 lei (about EUR 3,000) and given a further order to supply the information within 5 days.

A complainant, a rival municipal election candidate, complained that the sitting mayor had reused the contact details of about 476 citizens who had earlier asked him for help as mayor (2012-2018), cross-checking them with the electoral roll to send a campaign letter in October 2018. The Chambre Contentieuse found that this reuse was incompatible with the original purpose of collection, breaching Article 5(1)(b) and Article 6(4) GDPR. It imposed a reprimand and an administrative fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision with direct identifiers removed.

A former client of a veterinarian complained that the vet, who was an election candidate, used his client file to send electoral propaganda letters. The inspection service found that the vet admitted using the client list, 654 people, for the mailing. The Litigation Chamber held this was further processing incompatible with the original purpose, in breach of Articles 5(1)(b) and 6(4) GDPR. It imposed a reprimand and an administrative fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision in anonymised form.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation of Telekom Romania Mobile Communications SA on 25 November 2019, after a complaint from a person who kept receiving at home invoices addressed to another customer and got no answer when he told the operator. The operator could not show that the data it processed was accurate, which breached the accuracy principle. It also lacked suitable technical and organisational measures, so a customer's data was disclosed when invoices were sent to the complainant's address. The authority issued a warning for the Article 32 breaches and a fine of 9,544.40 lei (about EUR 2,000) for the Article 5(1)(d) breach.
The ANSDPC in Romania fined BNP Paribas because it did not respond to the applicant’s access request within the one-month period required under Article 12(3) GDPR.

The CNIL restricted committee sanctioned a French insulation and heat-pump company (named X in the published text) after a 2018 complaint about unwanted phone marketing. Its inspection found excessive comments about prospects in its customer software, including comments on health, calls recorded without notice, no effective opposition procedure, incomplete answers to the CNIL's document requests, and transfers outside the EU without safeguards. The committee imposed a fine of EUR 500,000, an injunction with a penalty of EUR 500 per day of delay, and publication of the decision for two years.

A former employee complained that his employer had sent 73 pages of call records for his work phone to his ex-wife, and that the employer had forwarded his private emails from his work mailbox after he left and had not closed the mailbox in time. Persónuvernd found that the disclosure of the call records had no legal basis under Act No. 90/2018 and that the handling of the mailbox did not comply with Regulation No. 837/2006 on electronic monitoring. No fine was imposed. The bankruptcy estate of the company was ordered to close the complainant's mailbox and confirm this to the authority by 14 December 2019.

The Romanian data protection authority finished an investigation into Globus Score SRL on 19 November 2019, started after an intimation. The company had ignored the authority's requests for information and was first given a reprimand with an order to send the information within 5 working days. It did not comply, so the authority fined it 9551.80 lei (about EUR 2000) for breaching Article 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR, and again ordered it to send the requested information.
The NAIH confirmed that the exercice of the access right and the accuracy principle do not require to provide certified copies to the data subject.
The AKI re-examined complaint about financial service provider’s incomplete response to data subject’s access request after appeal.
The AEPD imposed a fine of € 3,000 against the General Labour Union (GCT) for the violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.
The Ministry of Internal Affairs has been ordered to ensure a sufficient level of security regarding the personal data collected by automatic speed camera.

A user of an online classified-ads portal asked the operator to delete his profile, which was registered under a first name and an email address only. The operator refused to act unless he filled in a form with full name, address and past-contact details or supplied unspecified documents to prove his identity. The Austrian DSB held that this identity check went beyond what was necessary for a pseudonymous account, infringing the right to erasure under Art. 12(2) in conjunction with Art. 17(1) GDPR. It ordered the operator to delete the profile and its data within two weeks. No fine was imposed.
The AEPD imposed a fine of € 900 to Todotecnicos24h S.L for violation of Article 13 GDPR.

The Romanian authority closed an investigation into the airline TAROM on 7 November 2019, following the company's own personal data breach notification. It found that TAROM had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures: an employee accessed the booking application without authorisation, photographed a list with the data of 22 passengers and the list was disclosed online. The controller was fined 95,194 lei, stated to be equivalent to EUR 20,000, for breaching Article 32.
The ICO issued a decision on the necessity of a disclosure of information hold by a public entity to satisfy the legitimate public interests of accountability and transparency.
The AEPD approved Centros comerciales Carrefour S.A compliance with the GDPR after having used its investigation powers.
The AEPD approved a transport hub's compliance with Articles 32 and 33 GDPR after having used its investigation powers.
The AEPD confirmed an online pharmacy's (Promofarma ecom S.L) compliance with the GDPR after having used its investigation powers.
The AEPD held that an outdated privacy policy on a webpage violates Article 13 GDPR.

The Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL) followed the measures implemented by BOUTIQUE.AERO to prevent the excessive video surveillance of its employees and found that the controller was compliant with the GDPR. The CNIL closed the case.
The AEPD found that the El Maestro Cerrajero SL’s privacy policy complied with Article 13 GDPR, after the page was updated by the controller during the procedure.
The DPA ordered a bank (KUTXABANK S.A.) to respond to a subject access request.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation at the Bucharest branch of ING Bank N.V. Amsterdam, started after a referral. It found that the bank had not built adequate technical and organisational safeguards into its automated card-transaction settlement process (privacy by design and by default). As a result, the card payments of 225,525 customers were duplicated between 8 and 10 October 2018. The authority fined the bank EUR 80,000 for breaching Article 25(1) read with Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, also referring to Article 32(1)(d).
The IP issued an advisory opinion on the principle of data minimisation and on the processing which is necessary for the performance of a contract in the banking sector.
On 4 November 2019, the Slovenian DPA (IP) exercised its powers under Article 58(3) GDPR to issue an advisory opinion regarding requirements for a consent.
On 4 November 2019, the Slovenian DPA (IP) exercised its powers under Article 58(3) GDPR to issue an advisory opinion regarding processor's and controller's roles.
The Commissioner ruled that complaints about a property were the complainant's personal data and applied Regulation 5(3) of the EIR to prevent disclosure,
The ICO issued a decision, regarding disclosure of information which do not include personal data.
The ICO issued a decision regarding the refusal to access to third party personal data.
The ICO issued a decision regarding refusal to access to third party personal data.

This is not the decision itself but the authority's 2020 annual report, which briefly mentions the case. In November 2019 the Baden-Württemberg data protection authority fined a restaurant EUR 5,000 for extensive video surveillance with 24 cameras and 350 seats. The authority found the surveillance was not necessary to protect the controller's interests, since the stated reasons (protecting the buffet from poisoning by competitors) were not backed by facts or general experience. The report calls it a serious case of unlawful video surveillance. No formal reasoning, reference number or exact date is given.
The AEPD imposed a fine of € 6.000 for unlawful processing data from a public registry without a legal basis under Article 6 GDPR.

A complainant asked a public authority for copies of all documents from a recruitment process he had taken part in. The authority told all other applicants that he had made the request and that it intended to release their application documents to him, and it named him in that notice. The complainant objected that naming him was unlawful, unfair and disproportionate, and that he had not been informed of the disclosure. Persónuvernd found that the notice was lawful: the disclosure had a legal basis, was proportionate because the other applicants had an interest in knowing who received their data, and the authority had no duty under Article 13 GDPR to tell the complainant about it.

The Berlin data protection commissioner issued a fine of about EUR 14.5 million against the real estate company Deutsche Wohnen SE. On-site inspections in 2017 and 2019 found that tenants' personal data was kept in an archive system with no way of deleting data no longer needed, so years-old private and financial data was still stored. The company had been urgently advised in 2017 to change the system but had not fixed it by March 2019. The authority also imposed further fines of EUR 6,000–17,000 for 15 individual cases of unlawful storage. The decision was not yet final and could be challenged.

The Romanian DPA announced that on 28 October 2019 it finished an investigation into the courier company FAN Courier Express SRL. It found that the company had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational measures to secure personal data. Security incidents led to loss and unauthorised disclosure or access to personal data, including payment card and identity data, of about 1,100 people. The company was fined 52,325.9 lei, stated to be equivalent to EUR 11,000.
